title: Empires, Trade and Nations · Episode 1
chapters: The East India Company: a business that ruled
The Opium Wars and China's century of humiliation

units.t: Empires, Trade and Nations. Episode one.
In this episode: The Spanish Armada, 1588, The East India Company: a business that ruled, The Thirty Years' War and The Opium Wars and China's century of humiliation.
Part one. The Spanish Armada, 1588.
The most powerful empire on Earth sent a giant fleet to conquer England.
Fireships, bad maps and brutal storms decided what happened next.
A quarrel between monarchs.
Picture two rulers who had once been in-laws.
Philip II of Spain had been married to Mary I of England, Elizabeth I's older half-sister.
After Mary died, Elizabeth steered England firmly towards Protestantism, while Philip saw himself as the champion of Catholic Europe.
The quarrel deepened for decades.
English privateers such as Francis Drake raided Spanish treasure ships and colonies, and Elizabeth sent soldiers to help Dutch Protestants rebelling against Spanish rule.
The breaking point came in 1587, when Elizabeth allowed the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the Catholic cousin many hoped would replace her.
To Philip, invading England now looked like a matter of faith, security and honour all at once.
The grand plan.
The Armada that sailed in 1588 numbered around 130 ships, carrying sailors, soldiers, priests, horses and enormous supplies.
Its commander, the Duke of Medina Sidonia, was a wealthy nobleman with little experience at sea who had reportedly tried to decline the job.
The fleet could not conquer England by itself.
Its task was to sail up the English Channel, link up with the Duke of Parma's veteran army in the Spanish Netherlands, and protect the barges carrying those troops to Kent.
The flaw was plain in hindsight.
No deep-water port existed where the big ships and Parma's barges could safely meet, and messages between the two dukes moved slowly.
Coordinating them under enemy fire would prove almost impossible.
Fireships at Calais.
In late July 1588 the Armada was sighted off Cornwall and beacons flared along the coast.
It moved up the Channel in a disciplined crescent, with strong warships guarding the supply vessels at the centre.
The English, led by Lord Howard of Effingham with Drake as a senior captain, had faster ships and longer-range guns.
Spanish tactics relied on boarding, so the English kept their distance.
The Armada stayed largely intact and anchored off Calais.
On the night of 7 to 8 August, by the modern calendar, the English sent eight burning ships, packed with tar and pitch, drifting towards the anchored fleet.
Many Spanish captains cut their cables and scattered.
At Gravelines the English attacked closer, wrecking or capturing several ships and pushing the rest away from Parma.
The long way home.
With the wind from the south and the English behind them, the Spanish could not return down the Channel.
Medina Sidonia sailed north around Scotland and down the west coast of Ireland, a huge detour through unfamiliar, stormy waters.
The ships were battered and short of water and food, and their charts of those coasts were poor.
Autumn gales drove many onto the rocks of Ireland and Scotland.
Thousands of men drowned, and many who reached shore were killed or captured.
Historians think roughly a third or more of the fleet never made it back to Spain, and a far larger share of the men died.
Most of those losses came from weather, disease and hunger rather than from battle.
Legend and reality.
While the danger was still real, Elizabeth travelled to Tilbury on the Thames to review her troops.
Accounts record her saying she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, but the heart and stomach of a king.
Historians debate her exact words, because the best-known version was written down years later.
English propaganda presented the victory as God's favour and called the storms a Protestant wind.
The reality was messier.
The war dragged on until 1604.
An English counter-attack in 1589 failed badly, and Philip's later armadas in the 1590s were scattered by storms.
Spain stayed dominant in Europe for decades.
Yet the failure kept Protestant England independent, encouraged the Dutch revolt and gave English sailors confidence.
Its biggest legacy was a story of plucky defiance, retold in 1805, 1940 and beyond.
The key idea: The Armada grew from a religious and political feud between Catholic Spain and Protestant England.
Part two. The East India Company: a business that ruled.
It began as a group of London merchants chasing pepper.
Within two centuries it had its own army and ruled millions of people across India.
Merchants and a charter.
On the last day of 1600, Elizabeth I granted a charter to a group of London merchants, giving them the sole English right to trade with Asia.
Their target was spices, especially pepper.
The Company was an early joint stock venture: investors pooled money to fund risky voyages and shared the returns.
The richer, more aggressive Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, soon pushed the English out of the most lucrative spice islands in what is now Indonesia.
So the English turned to India, where they found something more valuable than pepper: cotton textiles.
Indian calicoes and chintzes became a fashion craze at home.
Its fortified trading posts, called factories, grew into Madras, now Chennai, Bombay, Mumbai, and Calcutta, Kolkata.
At first it depended on the favour of the Mughal Empire.
Betrayal at Plassey.
As Mughal power weakened in the 1700s, the Company began to use soldiers and money to play politics.
Bengal was among India's richest provinces.
In 1756 its young ruler, the Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah, captured Calcutta after the Company strengthened its fortifications without permission.
Robert Clive, an ambitious and ruthless Company officer, sailed north to retake it.
He found allies among Bengal's elite who wanted the Nawab gone, including his army commander Mir Jafar.
At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Clive's much smaller force faced the Nawab's army, but much of it never fought because its commanders had already agreed to switch sides.
Siraj ud-Daulah was later killed and Mir Jafar installed as a puppet ruler.
Huge sums flowed to the Company and to Clive personally.
Trader to tax collector.
The real turning point came in 1765.
The weakened Mughal emperor granted the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa: the right to collect land revenue across a vast, populous region.
Instead of bringing silver from Britain to buy Indian goods, the Company could now use Indian taxes to pay for them, and for its growing army.
Poorly supervised officials often grew rich through private trade and bribes, earning the nickname 'nabobs' back in Britain.
In 1770 a devastating famine struck Bengal.
Millions died, possibly as much as a third of the population in the worst areas, and critics accused the Company of making things worse by keeping up harsh tax collection while people starved.
Too big to fail.
By the early 1770s the Company was both mighty and in financial trouble, and Parliament grew alarmed that a private business was running an empire.
The Regulating Act of 1773 began bringing it under government oversight, and later laws created a government board to supervise its political decisions.
The 1773 Tea Act, meant to help the Company sell surplus tea in America, led to the Boston Tea Party.
Warren Hastings, the first Governor General of Bengal, was impeached in a seven-year trial and acquitted, but it showed British unease.
Meanwhile the Company fought wars against Mysore and the Marathas.
Most of its soldiers were Indian sepoys led by British officers, and its armies reached hundreds of thousands, larger than Britain's own.
It also grew opium for smuggling into China, to pay for Chinese tea.
Rebellion and the end.
In 1857 a mutiny by sepoys at Meerut spread into a widespread rebellion across northern India, fuelled by grievances from annexations and taxes to fears of religious interference.
The fighting was brutal on both sides, and the British response was savage.
Afterwards, Parliament decided the Company could no longer be trusted with India.
In 1858 the Crown took direct control, beginning the period known as the Raj, and the Company was formally dissolved in 1874.
By the 1850s it ruled much of the subcontinent directly or through treaties with princely states, with its trading monopolies stripped away.
Its legacy is debated.
It left cities, railways planned in its final years and words such as 'loot', borrowed from Hindi.
It also warns of a profit-seeking corporation holding unchecked political and military power.
The key idea: The East India Company began in 1600 as a monopoly trading venture and turned to Indian textiles after losing the spice islands.
Part three. The Thirty Years' War.
It began with three men thrown from a castle window and became one of the deadliest wars in European history.
Its peace treaties helped shape the idea of the modern state.
Out the window in Prague.
In May 1618, angry Protestant nobles stormed Prague Castle, seized two Catholic officials of the Habsburg emperor and their secretary, and threw them from a high window.
All three survived.
Catholics said angels saved them; Protestants said they landed in a dung heap.
The nobles were protesting Habsburg limits on Protestant rights in Bohemia.
They rejected their Habsburg king and offered the crown to a Protestant, Frederick V of the Palatinate.
Revolt spread easily because the Holy Roman Empire was a patchwork of hundreds of states, not a unified country, with an emperor of limited authority.
Religious tension, rival dynasties and foreign powers eager to weaken the Habsburgs made it a tinderbox.
Catholic victories.
Frederick V's reign was so brief he became known as the Winter King.
In 1620 imperial and Catholic League forces crushed his army at White Mountain, outside Prague.
Bohemia was forcibly returned to Catholicism, Protestant nobles were executed or driven out, and their lands went to loyal supporters.
King Christian IV of Denmark, a Lutheran who also held lands within the empire, intervened in 1625 but was defeated.
The emperor's armies were now partly led by Albrecht von Wallenstein, a brilliant and enormously wealthy military entrepreneur.
He raised his own huge army and paid for it by forcing occupied regions to supply money and food.
Sweden and France.
In 1630 King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, a Lutheran, landed with a disciplined army, mobile field artillery and flexible infantry.
Nicknamed the Lion of the North, he won at Breitenfeld in 1631, funded partly by Catholic France, which cared more about weakening the Habsburgs than about religion.
He was killed at Lützen in 1632, though Sweden won the battle.
Wallenstein, suspected of disloyalty, was assassinated by his own officers in 1634.
In 1635 France, guided by Cardinal Richelieu, openly entered the war, fighting alongside Protestant Sweden and German princes against the Catholic Habsburgs.
France feared being encircled by Habsburg lands.
The war was now mainly about the balance of power in Europe.
Hunger, plague and ruin.
Armies on all sides lived off the land, marching across the same German territories and plundering towns and villages again and again.
The worst single atrocity was the sack of Magdeburg in 1631, when imperial troops stormed the Protestant city and it burned.
About 20,000 people died, and the city was left almost empty.
Yet most deaths came from what armies brought with them: seized crops and livestock, burned farms, typhus and plague, and refugees crowded into towns where hunger followed.
Estimates vary, but many historians think German lands lost roughly a fifth or more of their population, with some regions losing far more.
Jacques Callot's etchings The Miseries of War and the novel Simplicius Simplicissimus captured the horror.
Westphalia and the state.
Peace talks dragged on for years in two Westphalian towns, Münster and Osnabrück.

The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederation, gave territory to France and Sweden, and allowed German princes greater freedom to run their own affairs.
Calvinism was finally recognised alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism; the 1555 Peace of Augsburg had let each ruler choose only Lutheran or Catholic.
Political scientists often trace 'Westphalian sovereignty' to here: the idea that states are equal and should not interfere in each other's internal affairs.
Historians say this is partly a later myth.
Even so, Europe shifted away from wars fought mainly over religion towards competing sovereign states.
The key idea: A window-throwing in Prague in 1618 ignited a revolt that spread across the Holy Roman Empire's patchwork of states.
Part four. The Opium Wars and China's century of humiliation.
Britain went to war so its merchants could keep selling a drug China had banned.
The consequences still shape China's view of the West.
Tea, silver and opium.
By the late 1700s the British drank enormous amounts of tea, almost all of it from China.
China wanted little that Britain made, and the Qing government confined Western merchants to the port of Canton, now Guangzhou.
So Britain paid in silver, and silver drained towards China.
The East India Company found a fix in Bengal, which it controlled.
It grew opium there and sold it at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who smuggled it ashore in China.
That kept the Company's own hands technically clean, and silver began flowing the other way.
By the 1830s tens of thousands of chests arrived each year, and addiction had spread from the wealthy to soldiers, officials and labourers.
Commissioner Lin's stand.
China had banned opium, but smugglers worked with corrupt officials.
Officials feared the harm to people and the army, and the silver drain, which made taxes harder for farmers to pay.
After a fierce debate over legalising or crushing the trade, the Daoguang Emperor chose to crush it.
In 1839 he sent an incorruptible official, Lin Zexu, to Canton.
Lin blockaded the foreign merchants until they surrendered more than 20,000 chests, after British superintendent Charles Elliot promised them compensation.
Lin had the opium mixed with lime and salt and flushed out to sea.
He also wrote to Queen Victoria, asking how Britain could allow a poison it banned at home to be sold to China.
Historians doubt she ever read it.
The First Opium War.
British merchants lobbied for war.
Some MPs, including a young William Gladstone, called it unjust and shameful, but the government sent a naval force anyway.
Warships such as the iron steamship Nemesis, which could navigate shallow rivers, destroyed Chinese junks and forts, and British forces threatened Nanjing.
Misleading reports meant the emperor did not grasp how badly it was going.
The Treaty of Nanking, 1842, was the first of the 'unequal treaties'.
China paid an indemnity, handed over Hong Kong Island and opened five ports, including Shanghai.
British subjects gained extraterritoriality, meaning trial under British law.
Strikingly, the treaty never mentioned opium, and the trade grew.
The Second Opium War.
Western powers wanted more access, including diplomats in Beijing and trade inland.
In 1856 Chinese officials boarded the Arrow, a ship registered in Hong Kong, and Britain used the incident to go to war again, this time with France.
Qing officials later detained and mistreated a British and French negotiating party, and some died.
In response, the British envoy Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace outside Beijing destroyed.
Troops looted its treasures, many of which remain in Western collections, and burned it.
The treaties that followed opened more ports, allowed foreign envoys in Beijing, ceded Kowloon to Britain and effectively legalised the opium trade.
A century of humiliation.
The wars weakened the Qing dynasty at a terrible time.
The Taiping Rebellion, which began in 1850, killed perhaps 20 million people or more, and further defeats and concessions followed for decades.
In 1898 Britain leased the New Territories next to Kowloon for 99 years, which set the stage for Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule in 1997.
In China, the period from 1839 to the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 is often called the century of humiliation.
It features in school textbooks and national messaging.
Many in the West know little about the Opium Wars, yet they help explain why China's leaders talk so often about sovereignty, foreign interference and national rejuvenation.
The key idea: Britain paid for Chinese tea in silver, then used Bengal-grown opium to win that silver back.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What lay behind the Spanish Armada?
Answer. A religious and political feud with England.
Question two. Why did the East India Company shift its focus to India?
Answer. Dutch rivals shut it out of the spice trade.
Question three. Why could a local revolt in Prague spread so widely?
Answer. It was a patchwork of states, with religious tensions.
Question four. How did the East India Company reverse the flow of silver to China?
Answer. By selling Bengal-grown opium to smugglers.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
